1.sense: The surah opens on a specific case rather than a general address: a woman has already brought her complaint, and Allah says He heard it before this verse was recited. The sentence pairs her plea to Allah with the exchange between her and her husband, and says Allah hears both.

notes.t: Qad with a past-tense verb sets the hearing as already complete before the recitation reaches the reader; the surah answers a report of anguish with a report of attention.
Allah had already ruled elsewhere that zihar does not make a wife a mother; this verse narrates the case that put that ruling to work.
A report names the woman as Khawla bint Tha'laba, with Aisha saying she caught only part of the plea while Allah heard it all; the chain is discussed by hadith critics.
notes.src: reports from Aisha, collected by Ibn Majah and others; grading disputed

links.why: the general ruling that zihar does not make a wife a mother, stated before this narrower case
Allah telling Musa and Harun He hears and sees them both, the same pairing of verbs

2.sense: Defines the practice the surah opened on: a husband likening his wife's body to his mother's, a pre-Islamic formula meant to put her out of reach without a real divorce. The verse denies the words any power, only the woman who gave birth to a man is his mother, and calls the formula itself denounced speech and falsehood, before closing on Allah's readiness to pardon it.

notes.t: Zihar invokes zahr, the back, the husband saying his wife is to him like his mother's back; the verse answers the formula on its own terms, by denying what it claims.
The same denial appears there in a list of things speech alone does not make real, zihar and adopted sons among them.
Munkaran and zūran stack two words for wrong speech, one denounced by any fair judgment and the other simply untrue, before the sentence turns to Allah's readiness to forgive it.

links.why: the same denial of zihar's effect, stated in general terms
another place a spoken formula is denied the power to remake a relationship, there adoption

3.sense: Sets the remedy. A man who pronounces the zihar formula and then wants to keep the marriage rather than let the words stand as a separation owes the freeing of a slave before the couple may touch each other again. The instruction is framed for the community as much as the man, and closes on Allah's awareness of what is done.

notes.t: "Going back on what they said" means resuming the marriage rather than repeating the zihar formula; the expiation is the price of undoing a divorce-like statement while keeping the wife.
The verse that follows sets out the two remaining steps of the same expiation, fasting and feeding, for whoever cannot free a slave.
Raqabah, "a neck," stands for the whole person in the Qur'an's manumission language across several verses; the freeing is named by the part that would have carried a yoke.

links.why: the fallback steps of the same expiation when a slave cannot be freed
the same wording for freeing a slave in expiation, there for an accidental killing

4.sense: Sets out the two fallback steps for whoever cannot free a slave: a fast of two consecutive months, then, if that too is beyond him, feeding sixty poor people. The stated purpose is belief made concrete in obedience to Allah and His messenger, and the whole sequence is named a boundary Allah has set, with a warning attached for those who reject it.

notes.t: The three steps run in strict order, freeing, fasting, feeding, each named only after the one before it is ruled out, so the verse legislates a ladder rather than a menu.
The preceding verse sets the first step, freeing a slave, for whoever is able.
Ḥudūd Allāh, "the limits of Allah," is the Qur'an's term for a boundary set by revelation rather than reasoned out; naming the expiation this way closes off adjusting it by preference.

links.why: the first step of the same sequence, freeing a slave
the same fasting expiation of two consecutive months for one who cannot free a slave

5.sense: Turns from one household to a general statement. Those who set themselves against Allah and His messenger meet the same disgrace earlier communities met, and this time it comes after Allah had sent clear signs, so the disgrace is not for lack of evidence. A humiliating punishment closes the sentence for those who reject it.

notes.t: Yuḥāddūna comes from ḥadd, a limit or edge, and pictures opposition as standing on the far side of a boundary from Allah and His messenger, the same root behind ḥudūd in the verse before it.
The same verb describes those who oppose Allah and His messenger, there named for the fire they earn.
Kubitū is repeated in its own clause, "disgraced as ... were disgraced," binding this community's fate to earlier ones by the bare repetition of one verb.

links.why: the same verb for opposing Allah and His messenger, with the fire named as the outcome
earlier communities plotting against their messenger before being seized, the precedent this verse invokes

6.sense: Extends the punishment named before into a scene: a day when Allah raises everyone at once and tells them what they did. Their own record survives their memory of it, since Allah kept count of what they let slip from mind, and the sentence closes on Allah as witness to everything, not only to this.

notes.t: Aḥṣāhu, "He counted it," is accounting language, the same root used for a tally kept exactly; what the doers forgot, the ledger did not.
The same day is described as people going out in scattered groups to be shown the result of their deeds.
The contrast sits in one line, Allah recorded it, they forgot it, with no verb of forgetting ever attached to Allah.

links.why: the same resurrection scene of deeds being shown rather than argued away
the same opening line repeated almost word for word, there about people who swear falsely before Allah

7.sense: Opens with a rhetorical question that expects agreement rather than doubt. Allah's knowledge reaches every private conversation: no group of three or five or any other number meets in secret without Him present as one more among them, wherever they are. The verse ends where the one before it did, on a day when they are told what they did.

notes.t: Rābiʿuhum and sādisuhum, "their fourth" and "their sixth," place Allah inside the count of the group rather than above it watching from outside; the language is one of presence, not surveillance.
Allah is described as nearer to a person than his own jugular vein, the same closeness stated without the arithmetic.
A companion verse asks whether they think their secret talk and private consultation go unheard; it does not, and messengers are named as present, recording it.

links.why: the same claim about secret talk being heard, with angels named as the ones recording it
the case this general statement is about to be applied to, people returning to a forbidden secret conversation

8.sense: Names people who were told not to hold secret conversations and went straight back to it, now filling their private talk with sin, hostility and defiance of the Prophet. When they come to him they greet him with a phrase Allah never used as a greeting for him, then privately dare Allah to punish them for what they say. Hell is named as answer enough.

notes.t: The greeting they used is reported as a play on "peace be upon you" twisted into a word for death, a courtesy turned into an insult while still sounding like one.

A hadith describes some visitors greeting the Prophet ﷺ with this distorted greeting; Aisha caught the insult and answered it, and the Prophet ﷺ told her Allah loves gentleness. Exegetes link the incident to this verse.
Nuhū appears twice in the verse, so the return to secret talk is described as a return to a thing already named and already stopped once.

links.why: the positive instruction that follows, secret talk done in righteousness instead of sin
the general rule on greetings, returning a greeting with one as good or better

9.sense: Addresses the believers directly and turns the previous complaint into an instruction. Private conversation itself is not the problem; what fills it is. Believers are told not to fill their secret talk with sin, hostility and defiance of the Prophet, but with righteousness and awareness of Allah, who is where the gathering on the last day leads.

notes.t: Bi-l-birr wa-t-taqwā answers bi-l-ithm wa-l-ʿudwān phrase for phrase, the same grammatical slot filled with its opposite, so the verse corrects by substitution rather than by bare prohibition.
The same pairing, birr and taqwā, is named as what believers should cooperate in, set against sin and enmity in the very next clause there too.
The verse closes on ḥashr, the gathering, tying private conversation now to public account later.

links.why: the conduct being corrected, the same three things named there as what a group's secret talk was carrying
the same word pair, righteousness and awareness of Allah, set against sin and enmity

10.sense: Answers a worry the previous instruction could raise: what about the secret talk that is still sin, the whispering a believer sees but cannot hear? That kind is named as Satan's doing, meant only to cause grief, and it is denied any power to harm except by Allah's leave. Trust is placed with Allah rather than with tracking down what was said.

notes.t: Najwā narrows here to one kind only, the whispering meant to unsettle, distinct from the ordinary private conversation the two verses before it were regulating.
A grief the believers are told not to be troubled by, there the scheming of open enemies rather than whispering.
The verse ends on tawakkul, trust placed in Allah, the standard answer the Qur'an gives to a harm that cannot be traced to its source.

links.why: the instruction on ordinary secret talk this verse narrows away from
a parallel reassurance that a scheme against believers cannot harm them without Allah's permission

11.sense: Moves to the manners of a sitting gathering, likely the Prophet's own assembly. Told to make room for someone else, believers are told to do it, and Allah answers with room made for them in turn. Told to rise and make way, they are told to do that too, and the verse closes by naming who is actually raised: those who believe, and further, those given knowledge, ranked in degrees.

notes.t: The verse runs two matched commands, make room and rise, each answered by Allah's own verb from the same root, fasaḥa answered by yafsaḥ, a courtesy repaid in kind rather than merely rewarded.
Knowledge is named there too as what sets a rank of standing before Allah apart, fear of Him rather than status among people.
Exegetes differ on whether "rise up" addresses making space at a crowded sitting or dispersing when the Prophet ﷺ wished to be alone, and whether the two commands describe one setting or two.
notes.src: reports collected by at-Tabari and others; readings differ

links.why: knowledge named again as what marks people out before Allah, there paired with fear rather than rank
another verse naming those with knowledge alongside Allah's own testimony, both singling the same group out

12.sense: Adds a condition to private audiences with the Prophet specifically: give something in charity before the consultation, not after. The verse frames this as better and purer for the one who does it, not as an obstacle, and closes by allowing that whoever finds nothing to give is not shut out, since Allah forgives, and is merciful.

notes.t: Bayna yaday, literally "between the two hands of," is the Qur'an's ordinary idiom for what comes before something; the charity is timed strictly ahead of the meeting, not alongside it.
The very next verse reports that this instruction was eased almost as soon as it was given.
Reports say the ruling stood only briefly, an hour or a day by some accounts, with only Ali ibn Abi Talib named as having acted on it in that window; sources differ on how long it lasted.
notes.src: reports collected in the tafsir literature, including from Ali ibn Abi Talib; details disputed

links.why: the same instruction eased in the verse immediately after

13.sense: Names what actually happened: the requirement felt like a burden, few or none acted on it, and Allah eased it before it became a real difficulty. The instruction narrows back down to obligations already known, prayer, zakat, obedience to Allah and His messenger, and closes again on Allah's awareness of what is done.

notes.t: The question opens with the same phrase the previous verse used, ṣadaqah bayna yaday najwākum, now turned into a question about hesitation rather than a command.
The instruction this verse relaxes was given only one verse earlier.
Reports differ on who, if anyone, gave the charity before the rule was lifted; some name Ali ibn Abi Talib as the only one who acted on it, others report that no one did.
notes.src: reports in the tafsir literature; accounts differ

links.why: the instruction being eased here, stated in full one verse before

14.sense: Turns to a different group, people who have taken as allies a community Allah is angry with. The verse places them nowhere, not counted with the believers and not counted with the people they befriended either, and adds that they swear to a lie knowingly, not out of confusion.

notes.t: Exegetes differ on the identity of "a people with whom Allah is angry," most naming the Jews of Medina and some naming hypocrites more broadly; the surah does not name them itself.
notes.src: readings recorded by at-Tabari and later exegetes

notes.t: "Neither of you nor of them" repeats the same preposition, minkum and minhum, so the sentence places the group by negation on both sides rather than by any positive description.
A related warning against taking Allah's enemies as allies, there addressed directly to the believers rather than described from outside.

links.why: the same warning against alliance with Allah's enemies, addressed directly rather than described
people described taking others as allies against the believers, in similar language

15.sense: States the consequence in the shortest terms the passage has used yet: a severe punishment, already prepared, and a plain judgment on what they have been doing.

notes.t: Aʿadda, "has prepared," sets the punishment as already made ready rather than merely threatened, the same certainty of tense the surah opened with in qad samiʿa.
Sāʾa mā kānū yaʿmalūn is a fixed formula the Qur'an repeats after naming a group's wrongdoing elsewhere; it closes a case rather than adding new information to it.

links.why: the same closing formula used for a different group who trade Allah's signs for a small price

16.sense: Names the mechanism behind the lie in the verse before: their oaths function as a shield, cover for turning people away from Allah's way while looking innocent under oath. A humiliating punishment answers a humiliation they tried to hide behind.

notes.t: Junnah is the ordinary word for a shield carried into battle; the image makes the oath a piece of equipment rather than a statement, used defensively.
The same phrase, "they have taken their oaths as a cover," describes the hypocrites there almost word for word.

links.why: the identical phrase describing the hypocrites' oaths, in the surah named for them

17.sense: Wealth and children, the two things this kind of person usually relies on, are named and denied any power against Allah. The sentence moves straight from that denial to their fate, named plainly as company kept in the Fire without end.

notes.t: Amwāl and awlād, wealth and children, appear together elsewhere in the Qur'an as the pair a person is tested by or leans on; this verse strips both of any use at once.
The identical claim, wealth and children availing nothing against Allah, is made about disbelievers in almost the same words.

links.why: the same claim about wealth and children in nearly identical wording

18.sense: Returns to the resurrection scene named earlier, now filled in with what these people do there. They swear to Allah the way they swore to other people in life, still convinced the habit will hold up as it once did. The verse answers that conviction flatly: they are the liars.

notes.t: Alā, translated "unquestionably," is an attention-word the Qur'an uses to mark a flat correction; it interrupts the sentence right before naming them liars.
The same scene, oaths sworn before Allah on the resurrection day by people denying they associated partners with Him.
The verse repeats the earlier verse's opening line word for word before diverging, so the reader arrives at the same day twice, first as a general warning and now as this group's own moment in it.

links.why: the same day named at the start of both verses, before this one narrows to what these people do in it
the same scene of an oath sworn before Allah on the day of resurrection

19.sense: Names what stands behind their forgetting: Satan has taken hold of them and pushed the remembrance of Allah out of reach. The verse gives them a name, party of Satan, and answers it with a verdict on that party as a whole, they are the losers, whatever they think they hold onto.

notes.t: Istaḥwadha ʿalā carries the sense of a full takeover, one party gaining complete mastery over another; the verb is stronger than ordinary influence.
"They are the enemy, so beware of them," a companion description of the same hypocrite party elsewhere in the Qur'an.
Ḥizb ash-shayṭān stands in direct opposition to a phrase the surah closes on at its very end, ḥizb Allāh, the party of Allah; the two names frame the second half of the surah.

links.why: the opposite party named at the close of the surah, the phrase this verse's naming sets up
another description of the same hypocrite party as a standing enemy

20.sense: Repeats the verb from the earlier verse naming the same opposition and gives it a final ranking. Standing against Allah and His messenger is placed at the bottom, among the most humiliated, with no further description attached.

notes.t: Al-adhallīn is a superlative, not the ordinary word for lowly; the verse claims the extreme of the category rather than a place within it.
The same charge, the same verb, opened the passage the surah has been building since; this verse gives it its final ranking.

links.why: the earlier verse naming the same charge, disgraced there rather than ranked lowest

21.sense: States the decree behind the ranking just given, in Allah's own words rather than reported speech. Victory belongs to Allah and His messengers as a settled matter, not a hope, and the reason given is what Allah is in Himself, strong, and mighty.

notes.t: The verse shifts into direct speech, "I will surely overcome," the only first-person quotation of Allah's decree in the surah, marking the claim as settled rather than described.
The identical promise, "Our soldiers will be the victors," is stated as a general law near the end of As-Saffat.
Qawiyyun and ʿazīz, strong and mighty, are given as the reason for the decree rather than as separate praise, the cause named right after the claim.

links.why: the same promise of victory stated as a general law
the party of Allah named as the victorious ones, the same theme this surah closes on

22.sense: Closes the surah on the opposite party from the one just named. Real belief in Allah and the last day rules out affection for anyone set against Allah and His messenger, and the verse insists on this even against the strongest ties a person has, parents, children, siblings, clan. What is given in return is named in full: faith written into the heart, strength from a spirit granted by Allah, gardens with rivers, and a mutual satisfaction between Allah and them.

notes.t: The verse lists four relations in ascending scope, father, son, brother, clan, the same ties Arabian kinship loyalty ran on, named to be set aside rather than dismissed as unimportant.
The same list of family ties is named as something that must not be loved more than Allah and His messenger and struggle in His way.
A companion instruction not to take Allah's enemies and your own as allies out of affection, addressed to the believers directly.

Ḥizb Allāh closes the surah answering ḥizb ash-shayṭān from the earlier verse; the same sentence shape, alā inna ... humu, is used for both, so the surah's two possible endings are set in matching frames.

links.why: the opposite party named earlier, in the same closing sentence shape
the same four kinship ties named as what must not outweigh Allah and His messenger
